title: Agnes (c. 304)
hookLine: a girl of about twelve who would not give up her faith; lambs are blessed on her feast

lines: LAMBS IN A CHURCH IN ROME.
cards: Lambs, carried into a church in Rome, and blessed. It happens on the feast of a saint named Agnes, at a church built over the place tradition says she was buried.
Their wool is later spun and woven into a pallium, a narrow band the Pope gives to metropolitan archbishops to wear over their vestments. It's a gentle ceremony for a story that isn't gentle at all.
Agnes was a girl, killed for refusing to give up her faith.

teach.b: One early witness is Ambrose, the bishop of Milan, in his book On Virgins. First, her age. Ambrose says she is said to have been martyred at twelve.
He finds it hard to take in: a cruelty that didn't spare even so young an age, and a faith that wasn't stopped by it. Second, the chains.

The officials brought out chains, Ambrose says, and they were too big; her hands were too small for them. Too young to be sentenced, he says, and yet ready to win. She stood, prayed, and bowed her head.

Augustine, preaching on her feast, noticed it: Agnes in Latin sounds like agna, a lamb, and in Greek it means pure. Artists picture her with a lamb in her arms, and the lambs in Rome are blessed on her day.

At Mass, just before communion, Catholics sing or say the Agnus Dei, Lamb of God, taking up the words of John the Baptist in the Gospel of John: "Behold the Lamb of God, behold him who taketh away the sin of the world."
A lamb is small, it doesn't fight back, and in that Gospel line it's the one who carries the world's sin. Agnes, small, refusing to fight and refusing to give in, became a picture of that Lamb.
Her name is read among the martyrs in the Roman Canon, along with Perpetua and Felicity.

how: Catholics keep the memorial of Saint Agnes in the Church's calendar; in Rome, lambs are blessed on her feast and their wool is used for the pallia given to metropolitan archbishops, and at every Mass the people say or sing the Lamb of God before communion.

games.q: you're Agnes, a young girl. the officials bring out chains to frighten you. what does Ambrose say she did?
o: stood, prayed and bowed her head.
games.why: Ambrose says the chains were too big for her small hands, and she stood, prayed, and bowed her head.

practice: Choose one young person you know, a child, a teenager, a student, and think about the pressure they live under: from friends, from screens, from grades, from people who want them to be someone they're not.
Hold them gently, the way the lambs are carried in Rome; you don't need to fix anything. If you pray, ask God to give them courage and keep them safe; if you don't, wish them strength.

wordCard.voice: Agnes. A Roman girl, said to have been twelve, who would not give up her faith, and whose name sounds like lamb. Today's word.
